card.title: How attention hides later tokens
card.question: how does attention hide later tokens?

brief.prose: Each token is stopped from seeing tokens to its right by blocking those positions before attention weights are computed. Blocked positions get zero weight, so only earlier tokens and itself contribute.

standard.prose: Line 45 checks whether PyTorch has a built-in fused attention function and stores the result in `self.flash`. Without it, lines 49-50 build a lower-triangular matrix of ones with `torch.tril`, sized block_size by block_size, and store it as the buffer `bias`. Line 67 computes the raw score matrix `att` of shape (B, nh, T, T), where row i holds token i's scores against every token. Line 68 slices the buffer to the current T and uses `masked_fill` to set every score where the buffer is 0, meaning the later positions, to minus infinity. Line 69 applies softmax across the last dimension, and minus infinity becomes a weight of exactly 0. Line 71 multiplies those weights by `v`, so later tokens add nothing to the output. When `self.flash` is true, line 64 skips all of this and passes `is_causal=True` to `scaled_dot_product_attention`, which applies the same causal masking internally. The code shown does not include that function's internals, so how it masks is not visible here.

detailed.prose: Line 45 checks whether PyTorch has a built-in fused attention function and stores the result in `self.flash`. Without it, lines 49-50 build a lower-triangular matrix of ones with `torch.tril` and register it as a buffer, so it moves with the module but is not trained. Line 67 computes the score matrix, where entry (i, j) is how much token i looks at token j. Line 68 slices the buffer to T by T and replaces scores with minus infinity wherever the buffer is 0, which is every j greater than i. Line 69 applies softmax, and exp of minus infinity is 0, so those positions get exactly zero weight and the remaining weights in each row still sum to 1. Line 71 multiplies the weights by `v`, so later tokens contribute nothing. Row 0 can only see itself, so it always has at least one finite score and softmax never gets an all-minus-infinity row. The slice to T means shorter sequences than block_size work with the same buffer. When flash is available, line 64 passes `is_causal=True` instead and the buffer is never created.

card.title: How --flags override train.py globals
card.question: how do my --flags end up changing train.py?

brief.prose: Your flags are read by a small script that train.py runs inside itself. It replaces train.py's variables with your values before training starts.

standard.prose: train.py runs this file with exec, so its code executes inside train.py's own namespace and edits train.py's globals. The loop visits each command-line argument in order. An argument with no equals sign is treated as a config file name, which is printed and then exec'd, so its assignments overwrite globals. An argument with an equals sign must start with --, and is split into a key and a value. The leading dashes are stripped from the key. The key must already exist as a global in train.py, otherwise a ValueError is raised. The value goes through literal_eval, so numbers and booleans become real Python types, and on failure it stays a string. An assert requires the new value's type to match the old one, then the global is overwritten. The call to exec in train.py is not shown here, so you would need train.py to see exactly where it sits.

detailed.prose: The file is not a module; the docstring says it is exec'd from train.py so that globals() is train.py's globals. That avoids prefixing every setting with config., as the docstring states. Arguments are processed left to right, so a config file can set values and a later flag can override them. Because config files are exec'd, they can run arbitrary code, not just assign names. A flag like --batch_size=32 reaches the key check, which only accepts names already defined. A typo therefore fails loudly instead of silently adding a variable. The type assert means --learning_rate=1 fails if the default is a float, since int is not float. A string value like --dataset=shakespeare fails literal_eval with ValueError and falls back to the raw string. A value containing a second equals sign would break the two-way unpacking of split.

card.title: When ckpt.pt gets written during training
card.question: when is ckpt.pt written?

brief.prose: ckpt.pt is saved during training, right after an evaluation, when the validation loss has improved. It is also saved after every evaluation if always_save_checkpoint is on, but never at step 0.

standard.prose: The write happens only inside the evaluation block, which runs when iter_num is a multiple of eval_interval and this is the master process. Evaluation first computes the losses and prints them. Next, the check on validation loss passes if the new val loss beats best_val_loss, or if always_save_checkpoint is true. When it passes, best_val_loss is updated to the new value. The save is skipped when iter_num is 0, so the initial untrained evaluation never writes a file. Otherwise a dict is built from the model weights, optimizer state, model_args, iter_num, best_val_loss and config. That dict is then written with torch.save to ckpt.pt in out_dir, overwriting any earlier file. The value of always_save_checkpoint is set elsewhere, and I would need the config defaults in train.py to say what it is by default.

detailed.prose: The write happens only inside the evaluation block, which runs when iter_num is a multiple of eval_interval and this is the master process. The check on validation loss passes if the new val loss beats best_val_loss, or if always_save_checkpoint is true. The save is skipped when iter_num is 0. The checkpoint holds the raw model state, the optimizer state, model_args, iter_num, best_val_loss and config, which is enough to resume training. It is written to the same path each time, so only the latest saved checkpoint survives. Note that best_val_loss is overwritten even when always_save_checkpoint caused the save, so it may go up. Only the master process reaches this code, which avoids several processes writing the same file.

iter 250: eval runs, say val 1.4 < 1.5, best_val_loss=1.4, ckpt.pt written

card.title: Warmup, cosine decay, then a flat minimum learning rate
card.question: how does the learning rate change over training?

brief.prose: The learning rate ramps up linearly at the start, then falls smoothly along a cosine curve. After that it stays at a small minimum value.

standard.prose: `get_lr` takes the step number `it` and returns the learning rate for that step. For the first `warmup_iters` steps, it returns `learning_rate * (it + 1) / (warmup_iters + 1)`, a straight-line rise toward `learning_rate`. Once `it` is past `lr_decay_iters`, it returns the constant `min_lr`. Between those two points, `decay_ratio` measures how far through the decay you are, from 0 to 1. The assert on the next line guards that range. `coeff` is half of one plus the cosine of pi times `decay_ratio`, so it slides from 1 to 0 along a smooth curve. The result is `min_lr + coeff * (learning_rate - min_lr)`, which starts at `learning_rate` and ends at `min_lr`. The values of `warmup_iters`, `learning_rate`, `lr_decay_iters` and `min_lr` are not defined in these lines, so I would need the config section of train.py or the config files to give numbers.

card.title: What the sample.py settings control
card.question: what do these settings do?

brief.prose: These are the defaults for generating text from a trained or pretrained GPT. You change them on the command line, for example `python sample.py --temperature=0.5`.

standard.prose: Line 12, `init_from`, picks the model: 'resume' loads your own checkpoint, or you pass `--init_from=gpt2-xl` to download a GPT-2 variant. Line 13, `out_dir`, is the folder your checkpoint is read from, and it is ignored for GPT-2 variants. Line 14, `start`, is the prompt text, and `--start="FILE:prompt.txt"` reads the prompt from a file. Line 15, `num_samples`, is how many separate texts you will see printed, and line 16, `max_new_tokens`, is how long each one is. Line 17, `temperature`, changes how random the text is: `--temperature=0.2` gives safer, more repetitive text and `--temperature=1.5` gives wilder text. Line 18, `top_k`, keeps only the 200 most likely next tokens, so `--top_k=10` narrows the choices further. Line 19, `seed`, makes the output repeatable: the same seed gives the same samples, and a new value like `--seed=1` gives different ones. Line 20, `device`, defaults to 'cuda', so without a GPU you must type `--device=cpu`. Line 21, `dtype`, picks bfloat16 if your GPU supports it and float16 otherwise, and you can override it with `--dtype=float32`. Line 22, `compile`, is off, and `--compile=True` makes PyTorch 2.0 compile the model, which adds startup time for faster generation.
